title: South Korea rides the AI boom – unevenly
gist: South Korea's economy and KOSPI have become far more concentrated in Samsung and SK Hynix as HBM demand from AI drove semiconductors to nearly 50% of exports in August 2026, mostly on price. Henry Storey flags social strains (housing, wage resentment), a US$520bn fab pledge under Lee Jae Myung's industrial plan, and risks from slowing AI demand and China's CXMT closing the HBM gap, while traditional industries lose attention.

insights.claim: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), made of vertically stacked DRAM chips, became essential for AI logic chips that need vast data delivered quickly, transforming commoditised memory into a strategic product.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Explains the structural shift in memory pricing power toward HBM leaders.

insights.claim: SK Hynix, which pioneered HBM, together with Samsung controls more than 70% of the global HBM market.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: A Korean duopoly dominates a critical AI bottleneck component.

insights.claim: The AI boom has diverted DRAM chips away from consumer electronics, causing steady 'chipflation' in memory prices.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Rising memory costs squeeze consumer electronics makers' margins.
insights.quote: The AI goldrush has diverted DRAM chips away from the consumer electronics market, leading to steady “chipflation

insights.claim: In August 2026, semiconductors made up nearly 50% of Korean exports, with shipment value tripling to nearly US$47 billion, driven almost entirely by price increases rather than volume.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Korea's export boom is price-driven and vulnerable to a memory price reversal.

insights.claim: SK Hynix and Samsung have consistently accounted for more than 50% of the KOSPI's value, making the index more reliant than ever on a few chaebols.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: KOSPI exposure is effectively a leveraged bet on the memory/AI cycle.
insights.quote: SK Hynix and Samsung have consistently accounted (Opens in new window) for more than 50% of the KOSPI’s value.

insights.claim: Surging semiconductor exports have reversed South Korea's historic trade deficit with China.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Korea's China trade balance now hinges on chip demand.

themes.theme: Social strains of the chip windfall

insights.claim: Samsung and SK Hynix semiconductor workers secured an annual bonus of US$400,000, even though less than 1% of Korea's workforce works in the chip sector.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Extreme wage concentration fuels inequality and political pressure for redistribution.
insights.locator: These developments have led to the rather surreal

insights.claim: The chip wealth influx has worsened housing unaffordability in the Seoul megalopolis, spawned chipmaking 'cram schools', and fuelled resentment where average wages, slowing outside the chip sector, hover around US$34,000.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Rising social polarisation could drive windfall-tax or redistribution policies.
insights.locator: The size and speed of this wealth influx

insights.claim: In May 2026, a close adviser to President Lee Jae Myung called for a 'citizen dividend' funded by AI wealth.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Early signal of possible future levies on AI/chip profits.
insights.locator: These problems have led to introspection

themes.theme: Industrial policy doubling down on AI

insights.claim: In June 2026, President Lee Jae Myung launched the 'Three Mega Projects for the Great Leap Forward' industrial policy built on semiconductors, data centres and physical AI, aiming to make Korea the world's number three AI power.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: State support for chips, data centres and robotics will continue to flow.

insights.claim: SK Hynix and Samsung pledged US$520 billion to build four huge chip fabs in southwestern Korea, and the 2027 budget includes over US$15 billion of supporting initiatives mostly for power and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Massive capex and grid buildout benefits equipment suppliers and power infrastructure, but raises oversupply risk.
insights.locator: As part of Lee’s policy announcement

insights.claim: Siting the new fabs in southwestern Korea, a progressive stronghold far from existing chip hubs, has prompted allegations of pork-barrelling.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Political site selection may raise costs and execution risk for new fabs.

insights.claim: Storey argues the greater risk is that Korea's AI focus diverts capital, talent and policy attention from traditional industries such as shipbuilding and EV batteries, which are far larger employers and where Korea is the main ex-China supplier.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Korean shipbuilding and battery makers' competitive positions could erode if neglected.
insights.quote: The greater risk may be that the focus on AI and enabling sectors diverts capital, talent and policy attention from traditional industries which are far larger employers.

insights.claim: Calls from frontier US AI labs for a deceleration in the AI development race caused anxiety on the KOSPI, raising the question of whether HBM demand will keep growing rapidly.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Any slowdown in AI capex is a direct downside risk for Korean memory stocks.
insights.locator: The growing calls emanating from frontier US AI labs

insights.claim: China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has become China's most valuable listed company and raised its global DRAM share to 10% from 4% a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Chinese DRAM supply growth threatens commodity memory pricing and Korean share.
insights.locator: China’s national champion for DRAM and HBM

insights.claim: With SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron prioritising HBM, US companies including Apple are testing CXMT chips for iPhones, causing concern among US senators.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Potential political backlash or restrictions on US firms sourcing Chinese memory.
insights.locator: Its global market share for DRAM

insights.claim: The Korea Semiconductor Industry Association reported in mid-September 2026 that Korea's HBM lead over CXMT has narrowed from five years to three years, though CXMT lacks access to ASML's most advanced lithography machines.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Narrowing HBM lead threatens future Korean pricing power; export controls are the key moat.

insights.claim: China has already eroded Korean market share across automobiles, shipbuilding, consumer electronics and petrochemicals.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests memory could follow the same path of Chinese share gains.
